title: Signals, Systems & Feedback Control
description: Continuous and discrete signals, linear systems, frequency response, feedback, stability, and controller design for sensors, actuators, and biological regulation.

modifications: Expanded week 1 with linearity and time invariance, impulse-response interpretation, zero-state transfer functions, pole and DC-gain calculations, units, and initial-condition and model limits. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcomes 1 and 2.

Expanded week 4 with sinusoidal magnitude and phase response, the first-order low-pass cutoff and decibel level, pre-sampling anti-alias filtering, and a worked alias calculation. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcomes 2 and 4.

Expanded week 8 with negative-unity-feedback algebra, closed-loop characteristic roots, sensitivity and disturbance paths, nominal stability versus performance, robustness limits, and the preserved gain-margin factor. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcomes 1, 3 and 4.

Expanded week 12 with proportional, integral and derivative action, conditional integral behavior under actuator saturation, anti-windup concepts, derivative noise, sample-and-hold implementation, quantization, and timing limits. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcomes 3 and 4.

Added an original discrete-time sequence linking a first-order difference equation to its impulse response, zero-initial-condition Z-transform, pole stability and proportional closed-loop pole; added eight formative items and four cards with synthetic values. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added a topic-level scope crosswalk comparing the combined course with MIT OCW 6.003 Fall 2011 and 2.004 Dynamics and Control II Spring 2008. It identifies their integration point and the Fourier, physical-system modeling, formal design and lab scope not developed locally; no lessons, questions or cards were added.

prerequisites.statement: Differential Equations; Linear Algebra; Circuits recommended

outcomes.description: Model systems with transfer functions or state space.
Interpret poles, zeros, and frequency response.
Tune feedback with attention to noise, saturation, and uncertainty.

lesson_objectives.description: Interpret the pole and impulse-response description of a simple LTI system.
Derive a first-order zero-state transfer function from a differential equation and calculate its DC gain.
Calculate the magnitude, phase and cutoff frequency of a first-order low-pass response at a stated sinusoidal frequency.
Explain why anti-alias filtering must precede sampling and calculate a simple alias frequency.
Derive the closed-loop transfer function for a single-input, single-output negative unity-feedback model.
Explain nominal stability, gain margin and robustness to model uncertainty without treating them as interchangeable guarantees.
Compare proportional, integral and derivative action, including conditions for integral removal of steady-state offset.
Explain how actuator saturation, sensor noise and digital sampling constrain an ideal controller model.
Model a heated chamber as a first-order system with a gain and a time constant, and write its transfer function.
Compute the closed-loop steady-state error and time constant under proportional control for a given gain.
Evaluate the effects of actuator saturation and integral action, and choose a gain with attention to noise and limits.
Compute the output of a discrete linear time-invariant system by convolving an input sequence with an impulse response.
Relate a first-order sensor's impulse response to its step response and time constant, and to its transfer function.
Quantify the lag and error a first-order sensor introduces for step and ramp inputs, and evaluate strategies to correct them.
Find the poles, the DC gain and the dominant time constant of a transfer function.
Use partial fractions to write and evaluate the step response of a stable system with real poles.
Apply the final value theorem and interpret zeros and poles in the right half-plane.
Compute the poles, damped frequency, overshoot, peak time and settling time of an underdamped second-order system.
Choose a damping ratio for a given overshoot specification.
Evaluate how damping and natural frequency shape the amplitude ratio of a measuring system at the frequencies of its signal.
Compute the magnitude in decibels and the phase of a first-order lag with a time delay at a given frequency.
Combine the magnitudes and phases of cascaded elements and convert a phase lag into a time lag.
Interpret the corner frequency, slopes and phase of a Bode plot and what a delay does to them.
Find the gain crossover and phase crossover frequencies of a loop with a lag and a delay.
Compute the phase margin, gain margin and delay margin, and the largest gain that keeps the loop stable.
Choose a controller gain for a target phase margin and relate the margin to the ringing of the closed loop.
Write a PI controller and compute its tuning for a lag-plus-delay plant by cancelling the plant lag.
Compute the crossover frequency and phase margin of the tuned loop, and the Ziegler–Nichols PI settings from the ultimate gain and period.
Explain integrator windup and the role of the derivative term, and choose where each is needed.
Compute the apparent frequency of a sampled component and the attenuation of a first-order anti-alias filter.
Estimate the phase margin lost to the zero-order hold and choose a sampling period for a loop.
Write the discrete PI update and the discrete form of a first-order plant, and compute them for given values.
Summarize step-test data by step size, counting runs and samples and averaging the settled response.
Estimate the gain, delay and time constant of a first-order-plus-delay model from step-response data and use them to tune a PI controller.
Evaluate what step tests of different sizes say about linearity and how that limits a tuning.
Explain, with the phase and the crossover frequency, why a measurement filter can turn a well-damped loop into an oscillatory one.
Compute the phase margin before and after the filter, the gain that restores a target margin, and the trade-off with noise.
Outline a retuning sequence that changes one thing at a time and verifies the measured margin, saturation and disturbance behavior before deployment.
Compute a first-order recurrence, impulse response and finite-time step response for a synthetic sampled system.
Derive a causal transfer function from a difference equation under zero initial conditions and identify its pole.
Classify discrete-time stability from first-order or proportional-feedback pole locations and interpret the natural response.
Build a Routh array for a closed-loop characteristic polynomial, find the proportional-gain range that keeps the loop stable, and count right-half-plane poles from sign changes.
Sketch a root locus from its construction rules and read design gains, breakaway points and imaginary-axis crossings from it.
Connect the stability limit to the gain margin and state what polynomial stability methods cannot handle, including time delay.

duration.equivalent_structure: Proposed 14-week undergraduate scope only. Week 13 now combines an original recurrence-to-Z-transform stability sequence with the existing sampling and discrete-PI lesson; week 11 remains a synthetic-data identification lab and week 14 a filter-retuning case. All activities are open, ungraded practice. There are no graded homework sets, exams or project, and workload has not been measured, so this schedule is not evidence of semester equivalence.

modules.title: LTI systems, convolution, and transfer functions

lessons.title: LTI systems, convolution, and transfer functions
lessons.worked_example: For dy/dt + 2y = 6u with zero initial condition, Laplace transformation gives G(s)=6/(s+2). The pole is s=−2 and the stable constant-input gain is G(0)=3, matching 2y=6u at steady state.

lessons.title: Frequency response and filtering
lessons.worked_example: A first-order low-pass with τ=0.05 s has cutoff fc=1/(2πτ)≈3.18 Hz. A 120 Hz tone sampled at 200 Hz folds to an apparent 80 Hz, so an analog anti-alias filter must act before sampling.

lessons.title: Feedback, stability, and robustness
lessons.worked_example: For negative unity feedback, y=G(r−y) gives T=G/(1+G). At a stated phase-crossover frequency where |L|=0.4, the simple nominal gain-margin factor is 1/0.4=2.5, subject to the model and crossover assumptions.

lessons.title: Controller design and sampled implementation
lessons.worked_example: For u(t)=Kp e(t)+Ki∫e(t)dt+Kd de/dt, a persistent error accumulates in the integral state. If the actuator is saturated, that state can keep growing without changing the applied output, then drive overshoot after the actuator leaves its limit.

lessons.title: Holding a culture at 37 °C: first-order plants, proportional control, steady-state error and saturation
lessons.worked_example: With K = 0.5 °C/W and τ = 600 s, holding 15 °C needs 30 W; K_p = 20 gives loop gain 10, error 1.36 °C and τ_cl = 54.5 s; K_p = 100 gives 0.294 °C, but start-up demands exceed the 50 W heater.

lessons.title: Convolution and impulse response: why a sensor blurs and delays what it measures
lessons.worked_example: Convolving the pulse [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0] with h = [0.5, 0.3, 0.2] gives [0.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.0, 0.0]; a first-order sensor with τ = 2 s shows 86.5% of a step after 4 s and lags a 0.5 units/s ramp by 1.0 units.

lessons.title: From a transfer function to a time response: Laplace transforms, poles, zeros and the final value
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic system with G(s) = 12/((s + 1)(s + 4)) has a DC gain of 3, the step response y(t) = 3 − 4e^(−t) + e^(−4t), a value of 2.459 at 2 s and a 2% settling time of 4.20 s; in the lesson, G(s) = 20/((s + 2)(s + 10)) has a step response of 0.5418 at 0.5 s and a settling time of 2.07 s.

lessons.title: Second-order systems: damping, overshoot and ringing in a pressure transducer
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic measuring line with natural frequency 10 Hz and damping ratio 0.4 has an overshoot of 25.38%, a peak time of 54.55 ms, a settling time of 159.2 ms and an amplitude ratio of 1.250 at 6 Hz; in the lesson, a 20 Hz line with damping 0.25 overshoots by 44.43% and doubles a 20 Hz signal.

lessons.title: Reading Bode plots: gain in decibels, phase, corner frequencies and the cost of a delay
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic plant with K 2, τ 4 min and a 0.5 min delay has a magnitude of −0.97 dB, a phase of −77.76° and a time lag of 2.714 min at 0.5 rad/min; in the lesson, G(s) = 0.5e^(−s)/(10s + 1) has −20.17 dB and −107.34° at the same frequency.

lessons.title: Stability margins: gain margin, phase margin and how much delay a loop can take
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic loop with G(s) = 1.2 e^(−2s)/(5s + 1) and K_p 2 has a gain crossover at 0.4363 rad/min, a phase margin of 64.6°, a gain margin of 1.911 and a delay margin of 2.585 min; in the lesson, the incubator loop with K_p 20 W/°C has a phase margin of 38.7° and a gain margin of 1.635.

lessons.title: PI control, tuning and integrator windup: removing steady-state error without losing the margin
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic plant with K 1.2, τ 5 min and θ 2 min, tuned with λ 3 min, has K_p 0.833, T_i 5 min, a crossover of 0.200 rad/min and a phase margin of 67.1°; in the lesson, the incubator tuned with λ 2 min has K_p 6.667 and a phase margin of 70.9°, while the Ziegler–Nichols PI settings give 30.6°.

lessons.title: Sampling, aliasing and a discrete-time PI controller
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic system sampled at 100 Hz with a 15 Hz first-order anti-alias filter shows 60 Hz interference at 40 Hz, attenuated to 0.2425; a closed-loop time constant of 5 min allows a sampling period up to 0.5 min, and a discrete PI update from e 2.0 to 1.5 gives 2.7083; in the lesson, a 0.5 min hold costs 4.77° of the 70.9° margin of the incubator loop.

lessons.title: Closed-loop poles as the gain changes: Routh–Hurwitz and the root locus
lessons.worked_example: For G(s) = 1/((s + 1)(s + 2)(s + 3)) with proportional gain K, the Routh first column 1, 6, (60 − K)/6, 6 + K gives stability for 0 < K < 60 and an oscillation at √11 ≈ 3.32 rad/s at the limit; K = 100 gives two right-half-plane poles. The locus has centroid −2, asymptotes at ±60° and 180°, and a breakaway at −1.423 (K = 0.385); ζ = 0.5 dominant poles −0.917 ± j1.588 occur at K ≈ 8.00. At K₀ = 20 the gain margin is 3, matching |G(j√11)| = 1/60.

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: identifying an incubator from step tests and checking a PI design
lessons.worked_example: In the synthetic step tests the settled gains are 0.499, 0.484 and 0.459 °C/W, the 20 W step gives a delay of 1 min and a time constant of 10.00 min, the cancellation tuning with λ 2 min gives K_p 6.803 W/°C, and the gain falls by about 8% across the range.

modules.title: Case: a filter that makes a loop oscillate

lessons.title: When a sensor filter makes a fast loop oscillate: phase lag, crossover and a safe retuning sequence
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic loop with K 1.2, τ 5 min and θ 2 min has a phase margin of 61.4° that falls to 43.5° when a 1.5 min filter is added, and a gain of 1.004 (from 1.0417) restores 45°; in the lesson, a 1 min filter takes the incubator loop from 51.8° to 26.9° and a gain of 8.68 W/°C restores 45°.

modules.title: Difference equations, Z-transform, and discrete pole stability

lessons.title: Difference equations, the Z-transform, and discrete pole stability
lessons.worked_example: For y[k]=0.75y[k−1]+0.25x[k] from rest, a unit step gives y[0:3]=0.25, 0.4375, 0.578125, 0.683594; the impulse response is 0.25(0.75)^k, H(z)=0.25/(1−0.75z⁻¹), and pole 0.75 is inside the unit circle.

grading_policy.attempt_policy: Unlimited formative retries; no summative grade is awarded.
grading_policy.solution_release: Public practice solutions may be shown after an attempt. They are not production exam keys.
grading_policy.late_policy: No deadlines or late penalties exist in this partial package.
grading_policy.appeals: No instructor review workflow is implemented; report ambiguous practice items to repository maintainers.

accessibility.diagram_policy: The seed package contains no imported diagrams; newly authored diagrams require descriptions and individual license tracking.
known_issues: Unicode equations require structured mathematical alternatives and assistive-technology review.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.

Added an original lesson on proportional control of an incubator (first-order plant, steady-state error, closed-loop speed, saturation and integral windup) with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added an original lesson on convolution, impulse response and first-order sensor lag with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Assessments with items now also list the course outcomes those items assess, derived from each item's lesson objective and that objective's outcome links. The rubric-only case lists none, and neither do the 4 prototype-unit assessments, whose objectives are not yet linked to an outcome. No readings, items or keys changed. The syllabus was regenerated from the manifest: it states the current version, lists every lesson with its item and card counts, and describes the current practice and limitations (it still described only the four original units). The course limitations shown to learners were also updated: they still described one formative check per lesson and the original numerical rules. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added a proposed 14-week schedule; seven original lessons (Laplace transforms, poles, zeros and the final value; second-order systems and damping; Bode plots, decibels and delay; stability margins; PI control, tuning and integrator windup; sampling, aliasing and a discrete PI controller; and a sensor filter that makes a loop oscillate, which prepares the course case on phase lag and a safe retuning sequence); and a synthetic-data lab on identifying an incubator from step tests. No new references were added. All activities remain ungraded practice; the package remains partial and unreviewed, gives no controller settings, safety procedure or test protocol for any real device, and makes no claim about any incubator, instrument or process.

Clarified both objectives and mapped them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcomes 1, 3 and 4. Added two MIT OpenCourseWare lecture pages as link-only references. Added an inactive digital-loop project draft combining aliasing, anti-alias attenuation, zero-order-hold phase cost, a sample-period constraint, a saturated discrete PI update and the exact sampled plant recurrence. The project is paper-only and ungraded; the package remains partial and formative-only.

Added an original week-13 sequence from a first-order difference equation through impulse response, the zero-initial-condition Z-transform, pole location and simple proportional-feedback stability. Eight formative items and four cards use synthetic values. The comparison follows MIT OCW 6.003 Fall 2011 discrete-time, feedback/poles and Z-transform sequence; the package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added a topic-level crosswalk for the combined signals/systems and feedback-control scope against MIT OCW 6.003 Fall 2011 and 2.004 Dynamics and Control II Spring 2008. It clarifies the local integration point and limits in Fourier analysis, physical-system modeling, formal controller design and laboratory work. No lessons, assessments or stable IDs changed; the package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added an original Routh–Hurwitz and root-locus reading grouped with the week-8 feedback lesson, following MIT OCW 2.004 Spring 2008 lectures 25–29: the coefficient test as necessary only, Routh arrays and sign changes, proportional-gain limits and the auxiliary polynomial, root-locus construction rules, reading a damping-ratio gain, and the equivalence of the Routh limit with the gain margin, with delay stated as a limit. Three objectives, eleven formative items and four cards; the crosswalk and syllabus record the new coverage. No week was added. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

limitations: All four preserved prototype readings now have expanded instruction beside original lessons and one synthetic-data virtual lab; this package is not equivalent to a full university semester.

A proposed 14-week schedule exists but is unmeasured and unreviewed. There is one synthetic-data virtual lab and no substantive homework sequence, laboratory sequence, midterm or cumulative final. An inactive integrative project draft is not scheduled or graded.

Practice items are short formative checks (two per prototype unit and six to nine per original lesson); they do not demonstrate comprehensive outcome coverage or mastery, and objective associations remain provisional.
Bloom labels and structured prerequisite edges are initial authoring classifications awaiting subject-matter review.
Question answers and solution feedback are intentionally public practice authoring specifications, not restricted exam keys.

Of the 74 numerical answers in this package, 18 require a unit, one checks significant figures and none checks dimensions; the others accept a number within a stated tolerance, with the unit optional.
Total workload and weekly duration are unknown; former nominal credit values and hardcoded reading times do not establish workload.

All plants, signals, controllers and numbers are synthetic teaching examples; this package gives no controller settings, safety procedures or test protocols for any real device and says nothing about any real incubator, instrument or process. The models are simplified textbook descriptions, not design methods for real equipment.

The new discrete-time unit is a first-order foundation with one proportional-feedback example; it does not add the Fourier, discrete-frequency-response, broad transform-property, controller-synthesis or nonlinear-system depth of MIT 6.003.

The local single-input/single-output sequence combines selected 6.003 signals-and-systems and 2.004 physical modeling/control topics. It does not cover the complete Fourier sequence, electrical/mechanical component modeling, root-locus design, hands-on implementation or lab depth of those comparators.
intentionally_omitted: Graded assessments, an activated integrative project and a laboratory sequence are not authored yet (one synthetic-data virtual lab exists); the original lessons extend a partial package.
A full discrete-time signals-and-systems sequence, including Fourier representations, discrete-time frequency response and broad Z-transform techniques, remains outside this bounded addition.
